parts.title: Campus Conversation: Asking for More Time
script: Listen to a conversation between a student and her history professor.
Hello, Professor Lee. Do you have a few minutes?
Of course, Sara. Come in. What can I do for you?
It's about my history paper. The one about the old trade roads. It is due on Friday.
Well, I was sick last week. I had the flu, and I stayed in bed for five days. So I am behind. I need more time to finish the paper.
I'm sorry to hear that. Are you feeling better now?
Yes, much better, thank you. But I only wrote two pages. The paper needs to be eight pages.
I see. Did you go to the health center when you were sick?
Yes, I did. The doctor gave me a note. Here it is.
Thank you. OK, this is fine. I can give you one more week. So the new due date is next Friday.
Oh, really? One more week? That's great. Thank you so much.
You're welcome. But I have one idea for you. The library has a writing center. Students there can read your paper and help you make it better. It's free.
A writing center? I didn't know about that.
Many students don't. It's on the second floor of the library. You should make an appointment early, because it gets busy before exams.
OK. I'll go there tomorrow morning.
Good plan. And Sara, if you have more questions, just send me an email.
I will. Thanks again, Professor Lee.

o: To ask about the final exam
To ask for more time to finish her paper
To change the topic of her paper
To get a book from the professor

questions.exp: She says, 'I'll go there tomorrow morning' about the writing center.

parts.title: Academic Lecture: How Honeybees Share Information
script: Listen to part of a lecture in a biology class.
Good morning, everyone. Today we will talk about honeybees. Specifically, how honeybees tell other bees where to find food.
Honeybees live together in a big group called a colony. One colony can have thousands of bees. Some of these bees have a special job. They fly out and look for flowers. We call these bees scouts.
When a scout finds good flowers, it flies back to the hive. But how does it tell the other bees where the flowers are? Bees can't talk, right? Well, the answer is: they dance.

Yes, they dance. There are two main dances. The first one is the round dance. The bee moves in a small circle. This dance means the food is close to the hive, usually less than about fifty meters away.

The second dance is the waggle dance. This one is used when the food is far away. In the waggle dance, the bee walks in a straight line and shakes its body from side to side. Then it turns and does it again.

The waggle dance gives two pieces of information. First, the direction of the straight line shows the direction of the food. Second, the length of the waggle shows the distance. A longer waggle means the food is farther away.
Now, who discovered this? A scientist from Austria named Karl von Frisch. He studied bees for many years, and in 1973 he won the Nobel Prize for this work.
Isn't that amazing? A tiny insect with a kind of language. OK, so for next class, please read chapter six. It talks about other insects that live in groups, like ants.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
o: How honeybees tell other bees where food is
How to keep bees at home
questions.exp: The professor says, 'Today we will talk about... how honeybees tell other bees where to find food.'

o: A bee that looks for flowers
A bee that guards the hive
questions.exp: Scouts are the bees that fly out and look for flowers.

questions.q: What does the round dance mean?
o: The food is close to the hive
There is danger near the hive
questions.exp: The round dance means the food is close, less than about fifty meters away.

questions.q: According to the professor, what does a longer waggle mean?
questions.exp: 'A longer waggle means the food is farther away.'

questions.q: Listen again: "Bees can't talk, right? Well, the answer is: they dance." Why does the professor say "Bees can't talk, right?"
o: To introduce the surprising answer to his question
To say that bees cannot share information
To ask students to stop talking
To change the topic of the lecture
questions.exp: He asks a simple question first so he can give the surprising answer: bees dance.

questions.q: How does the professor organize the information about bee dances?
o: He tells a story about his own bees
He describes two dances and explains what each one means
He lists the dances by date of discovery
questions.exp: He explains the round dance first, then the waggle dance, and what each means.
